Legal AI Engineering

Building Private, Defensible AI for Law

Elephant Scale

Two Questions You Will Be Asked

“Where did that document go?”

“Prove the system did what you say it did.”

Someone will ask you both. Opposing counsel, a judge, a client’s GC, a CISO, a state regulator, a CJIS Systems Officer.

By tomorrow evening you will have built a system that answers both — and you will walk out with the artifacts that are the answers.

Open here, on the two questions. Do not open with “AI is transforming legal.” Everyone in the room already believes that; it buys nothing. The two questions are the course. Write them on the board and leave them there for the whole course — every lab gets tied back to one of them.

Ask who has already had to answer a client security questionnaire about an AI feature. The hands that go up are your allies for the rest of the course.

Prerequisites and Expectations

  • You can write Python and call an API
    • Labs are Python; nothing exotic, no ML framework, no model training
    • If you can read a for loop and a requests call, you can do every lab
  • Bring your own AI subscription
    • A frontier assistant you already pay for — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or equivalent
    • Use it on the labs. We build AI for lawyers; we do not write code like it is 2019
    • No lab depends on it, and no lab needs an API key
  • No legal background required
    • Privilege, responsiveness, elusion, TAR, load files, custodians — taught in context, at the moment each one first costs you something as a builder
  • No ML background required
    • We build the mental model from the API surface down, not from the math up
  • Curiosity, and skepticism
    • Argue with me. Every claim in this course should survive being challenged, because in this field it eventually will be — under oath

Say the “no legal background” line explicitly and early. Engineers moving into legal tech are often quietly worried that the room will assume knowledge they don’t have. Defuse it in the first five minutes and you get real questions for the rest of the course instead of silence.

Our Teaching Philosophy

  • Emphasis on concepts and fundamentals — the primitives outlive the products
  • Highly interactive — questions and disagreement welcome at any moment
  • Hands-on — learn by doing; the labs are half the course
  • Taught from the builder’s seat — the instructor ships a real on-prem eDiscovery platform (FreeEed) and teaches AI security; you build your own pipeline in the labs, designed against that architecture rather than against a demo
  • Honest about limits — you will see a local model lose to a cloud model, in front of you, and we will talk about what to do about it

The “builder’s seat” line is the differentiator. Say it once here, then stop claiming it and start demonstrating it — the Tika/PST/OCR war stories in Module 2 and the egress attestation in Module 5 do the work.

Analogy: Learning To Fly…

You can read about flying all day. At some point you have to sit in the seat.

+ Flight Time

The labs are the flight time. The labs are not illustrations of the lecture; the lecture is preparation for the lab.

One System, Seven Labs

The labs are not seven exercises. They are one system, built in seven steps.

  Lab 02  messy corpus      ->  catalog.jsonl   (ingest, extract, OCR, dedupe)
  Lab 03  catalog.jsonl      ->  search index    (find anything inside everything)
  Lab 04  search index       ->  RAG + citations (answers you can go check)
  Lab 05  RAG                ->  local + attested (the boundary, proven)
  Lab 06  local RAG          ->  measured review (recall, elusion, precision)
  Lab 07  measured review    ->  scored + packaged (SAIS-100, on-prem bundle)
  Lab 08  all of it          ->  CAPSTONE: your portfolio project

Every lab consumes the previous lab’s output. Break step 2 and step 5 doesn’t run — which is also true of the real thing.

At the end you do not have notes. You have a running system and the evidence file that defends it.

Show this early and refer to it at every lab hand-off (“you are here”). The compounding structure is the single biggest reason this course lands better than a topic-per-module AI course. It also creates real stakes: a student who skips Lab 03 feels it in Lab 04.

Warn them now: if they fall behind, the fix is to take the reference output from the previous lab (shipped in every lab folder) and move on. Nobody gets stranded.

You leave comfortable in the area, holding a system you can show someone.

Show this slide before the first lab. It reframes the labs from “exercises” to “deliverables” and it is the slide people photograph. The right-hand column is also, almost word for word, the list of things a legal-tech hiring manager asks about.

The three after-class items are commitments, so say them plainly and do not embellish them. Six months of email support means the instructor’s own inbox, and six months of updates means they keep getting the current labs — which matters in a field where the regulations moved twice while this course was being written.

Say the no-client-data line out loud rather than letting them read it. Somebody will paste a privileged document into a support thread to show you why their extraction is failing, and the moment to prevent that is now, not then. Frame it as the course’s own rule applied to the course: if the argument for local AI is that privileged material should not land in someone else’s inbox, that includes mine.

The Shape of the Course

Core · Day 1 — Build the foundation: ingest, search, retrieve

  1. The legal engineer’s landscape
  2. Legal data is messy — ingestion and extraction
  3. Search and retrieval — the foundation
  4. RAG for legal documents — with citations

Core · Day 2 — Make it private and defensible

  1. Privacy, privilege, and local serving — the privilege trap
  2. Defensible AI review
  3. Capstone

Deep Dive — one day, scheduled separately: ship it, oversee it, prove it

  1. Ship it — workflow, private deployment, and governance
  2. Agentic and multi-step legal workflows (deep)
  3. Governance and compliance deep-dive

Electives, booked on their own or added to the Deep Dive — investigations (entities, relationships, timelines) · deployment at scale (CJIS, government, higher-ed)

Ground Rules

  • Ask the question when you have it. Not at the end.

  • The parking lot is real. Anything jurisdiction- or matter-specific goes on the board and gets answered before we close.

  • No client data in any tool during this class. Not a document, not an extract, not a “scrubbed” sample. Everything we use is synthetic and generated on your own machine. Module 5 is ninety minutes on exactly why — do not make it a live demonstration.

  • If I don’t know, I will say so. This field is eighteen months old. There are real open questions and I would rather name them than paper over them.

The third rule matters more here than in any other course we teach. Someone will be tempted to bring a real PST to Lab 02 “to see if it works.” The answer is no. The reason becomes Module 5. If they want their own data processed, they install FreeEed afterwards and run it on their own machine, which is the entire point of the product.

About the Instructor

  • Ten-plus years in eDiscovery — ingestion, processing, review, production
    • Not AI for legal observed from the outside. The unglamorous parts, from inside the pipeline — which is why Module 2 exists at all
  • Author of FreeEed — the open-source, on-prem eDiscovery platform
    • Every Tika / PST / OCR / load-file war story in this course is one I own in a bug tracker
  • Ten-plus years of technical training — Big Data, Hadoop, Spark, and now AI
    • Guide to Big Data Applications (Springer, 2017), HBase Design Patterns (2015), Hadoop Illuminated (2012); technical reviewer for Manning and Packt
    • Certified Google Trainer
  • A law degree — earned online, in order to build the software
    • Not a detour that happened alongside the work. A deliberate decision that you cannot build eDiscovery software on a second-hand understanding of what the law requires
    • I am not a lawyer, I am not your lawyer, and nothing here is legal advice
  • Author of Legal AI Engineering — the material you are holding

I ship the thing I am teaching you to build. When I tell you a local model loses to a cloud model, it is because I have watched it happen on my own hardware.

Keep this to ninety seconds. The room does not want a resume; it wants one reason to trust you for the next two days. That reason is the second bullet — you maintain an eDiscovery platform, so the failure modes in Module 2 are yours, not a vendor’s slide deck.

The law-degree bullet carries more weight than it looks. The point is the word for — the degree was taken to build the software, not collected along the way. That is the whole thesis of the course in one biographical fact: the legal requirements are not a wrapper you put around a working pipeline afterwards, they are an input to the design. Say it that way.

Then say “not a lawyer, not your lawyer, not legal advice” out loud and move on quickly. In a room that may contain actual lawyers, claiming less than you could is the only safe direction — and it buys credibility rather than spending it.

Do not oversell the books. They are Big Data books, not legal-AI books; the honest framing is “I have been teaching engineers hard things for a decade,” not “I am a published legal AI authority.”

About You

  • About you
    • Your name, and what you build
    • Are you coming from software into legal, or from legal into software?
    • What touches your system today: documents? email? scans? a review team? a court?
    • Your familiarity with LLMs (1–4; 1 = new, 4 = shipped something into production)
    • What you personally want to walk out with

   

Capture the “what do you want to walk out with” answers on the board and check them off at the close. Cheapest engagement device in the course.

The software-vs-legal split matters for pacing: a room of legal-tech engineers needs less Module 1 and more Module 6; a room of software engineers needs the opposite. Ask, then adjust the clock, and say out loud that you are adjusting it.

Where Are You On This Curve?

Quick poll, hands up:

  • My company has no AI in the product
  • We have AI in the product and it calls a cloud model
  • We have AI in the product and we have had to answer a client security questionnaire about it
  • We run a local model in production
  • We have had to defend an AI-assisted process to opposing counsel or a court

And the second question: can you, today, prove where a given document went?

Do this literally. The second question is the interesting one. Almost nobody can, and the gap between “we’re careful” and “we can prove it” is the commercial opportunity this entire course is about. Land that, then move.
